source_refs.note: Book p. 103: heading 3.7 Application of Definite Integrals (followed directly by 3.7.1); overview of the section is ours

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The book prints the heading 3.7 and goes straight on to 3.7.1, so this page only gives the plan of the section (our own overview).
Until now we have learnt how to evaluate a definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). In this section we use it to measure real quantities:
1. 3.7.1 Area under a curve, and the area between two curves.
2. 3.7.2 Consumer surplus and producer surplus in economics (areas between a demand or supply curve and a price line).
3. 3.7.3 Volumes of solids made by revolving a region about an axis, and volumes found from cross-sections.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The one idea behind all three: cut the quantity into very thin pieces, find the size of one typical piece, and add all the pieces with an integral.
A thin vertical strip of width \(dx\) and height \(f(x)\) has area \(f(x)\,dx\), so the whole area is \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).
A thin disk of radius \(f(x)\) and thickness \(dx\) has volume \(\pi[f(x)]^2\,dx\), so the whole volume is \(\int_a^b \pi[f(x)]^2\,dx\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. A definite integral adds up infinitely many thin pieces; that is why it measures area, surplus and volume.
2. Before integrating, always draw a rough sketch: it shows the limits, which curve is on top and where the curve crosses the axis.
3. Area and volume are never negative; a negative integral only tells you the region is below the axis.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Integrating without a sketch and using the wrong limits.
2. Reporting a negative number as an area.
3. Forgetting the units: area is in square units, volume in cubic units, surplus in rupees.
